meeting_header: Date: 2025-08-15 | Start: 16:30 PDT | Duration: 42 minutes | Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Samir Rao (NovaTech CTO), Leah Kim (NovaTech Sr ML Eng), Priya Das (NovaTech PM)
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked NovaTech through Hosted API chat and text generation basics: streaming responses, key parameters (temperature/top_p/max_tokens), retry/backoff recommendations, and example SDK/curl usage. Customer is evaluating hosted option first; interested in latency/cost tradeoffs and SOC2/security docs. Agreed next steps: pricing, sample prompts, benchmark snippets, and POC scoping call.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, we can get started. Quick intro - I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, Jordan's our SE.
[00:08] Samir Rao: Hi, Samir here. Leah and Priya on the line too. Thanks for doing this.
[00:12] Jordan Lee: Hi team. Today's plan is a quick walkthrough of the Hosted API for chat/text gen - streaming, main params, and how we recommend retries and backoff. We'll show the console and a live curl demo.
[00:25] Leah Kim: Sounds good. We're primarily concerned about latency and cost, and whether we can get streaming tokens to reduce perceived latency.
[00:35] Jordan Lee: Totally, that lines up - streaming is where you see the UI feel really snappy. We'll show server-sent events streaming and the SDK streaming clients. Also how to tune temperature/top_p for deterministic vs creative output.
[00:49] Maya Patel: Quick qual question - what's your current stack? Are you using a managed API already, or self-hosted models?
[00:56] Samir Rao: We use a mix - some inference on GCP VM pools, but most of our prototype calls go to external APIs. We want something more predictable and cheaper per-token.
[01:08] Jordan Lee: Cool. Hosted API can help there, we have different model tiers and a catalog. For demos we'll use a mid-capacity chat model - shows lower latency but reasonable cost.
[01:21] Jordan Lee: (shares screen) Here's the console: call playground, model selection, and the streaming toggle. You can see an example response streaming in chunks - each chunk is a partial event.
[01:33] Jordan Lee: Demo curl: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat --header "Authorization: Bearer <KEY>" -d '{"model":"redwood-chat-medium","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Write a short email about the outage."}],"stream":true,"temperature":0.2}'
[01:52] Leah Kim: We had a question earlier - how do you recommend setting temperature and top_p for customer-facing templates vs brainstorming?
[01:59] Jordan Lee: Good one. For deterministic templates keep temperature 0-0.3 and top_p around 0.8-1. For creative brainstorming bump temperature to 0.7 or higher, and maybe lower top_p if you want focused creativity. Also, set max_tokens to cap cost.
[02:16] Maya Patel: And about retries - we see occasional transient errors with cloud APIs. What's Redwood's guidance?
[02:22] Jordan Lee: We recommend idempotency keys at the request level for non-stream requests. For streaming, do simple retry on connection drop with exponential backoff, start with 500ms, double each time, max 5 retries. Also use our SDKs which have retry hooks built-in.
[02:40] Samir Rao: Any rate limiting? If we burst, will calls get 429s or queue up?
[02:46] Jordan Lee: Hosted API enforces per-account rate limits, you can request higher throughput. We return 429 with Retry-After headers when you hit the limit. For predictable throughput we recommend Redwood Dedicated, but hosted can handle steady QPS up to your tier.
[02:59] Priya Das: What about chunk loss in streaming? If a client drops mid-stream do we get partial outputs?
[03:05] Jordan Lee: Yes, streaming is best-effort. If you need guaranteed complete responses, use non-stream mode and ask for the full payload. For UX, we often combine streaming partials and a final response event that has the full text. Slight note - sometimes the transcript shows the KV cache as "K-V cash" in logs, small transcribe quirk.
[03:27] Leah Kim: Heh, noted.
[03:30] Jordan Lee: Quick demo of SDK: node snippet - const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.RW_KEY }); const stream = await client.chat.stream({ model: 'redwood-chat-medium', messages, temperature:0.2 }); stream.on('data', chunk => console.log(chunk.text)); stream.on('end', () => console.log('done'));
[03:50] Samir Rao: Do you support function/tool calling? We have ingestion pipelines that could be triggered.
[03:56] Jordan Lee: We do support structured outputs and function calling patterns. For hosted we'll run the model and return structured JSON that your integration can interpret. Note that function calling may change token counts slightly.
[04:07] Maya Patel: Pricing question - how do tokens map to cost for streaming vs non-streaming?
[04:12] Jordan Lee: Cost is per token consumed by the model. Streaming doesn't change cost - it just changes how you receive tokens. Keep an eye on max_tokens and prompt length. We can send a region-specific pricing sheet after this.
[04:29] Priya Das: Security - SOC 2, SSO, and data retention?
[04:34] Maya Patel: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II. We support SAML SSO, RBAC, and customer-configurable retention policies for hosted logs. For strict compliance we have Private deployment options. We'll share the security FAQ.
[04:48] Samir Rao: Great. For the demo could you show how retries look in practice?
[04:52] Jordan Lee: Sure - I'll simulate a dropped connection and show the SDK reconnect. (Jordan fakes a network hiccup) You can see the client resumes or retries a new request depending on mode. For streaming we re-request from the user side or re-run with the same prompt and idempotency key if it's safe.
[05:11] Jordan Lee: Also mention model fallbacks - if your preferred model is busy we'll fall back to a compatible variant. That is configurable.
[05:20] Leah Kim: How about batching? We have a bunch of requests - can you batch small prompts to save tokens?
[05:26] Jordan Lee: We support server-side batching for throughput, and caching for repeated prefixes (prefix caching / KV cache). That reduces per-token cost.
[05:33] Samir Rao: Any gotchas with streaming+function calling?
[05:38] Jordan Lee: The main caution is ordering of events; your function handler should be idempotent and handle partial outputs. For critical ops we recommend non-stream sync calls.
[05:48] Maya Patel: If it's okay I'll show a quick example prompt tuning and parameter sweep in the console.
[05:52] Jordan Lee: (shares screen) In the playground you can run a few calls with different temperature and see side-by-side responses. This is useful for setting guardrails before a POC.
[06:10] Priya Das: For the POC we expect about 150 QPS peak for generation and 20 QPS for embeddings. Is hosted going to be sufficient?
[06:19] Jordan Lee: 150 QPS sustained may push you towards Dedicated depending on model size and latency targets. Hosted can handle bursts and typical mid-level throughput, but for guaranteed SLOs Dedicated is recommended. We'll put some numbers in the spreadsheet.
[06:32] Leah Kim: Could you share the curl examples for chunked streaming and the non-stream variant?
[06:36] Jordan Lee: Yep. I'll paste both in the follow-up message. Example non-stream: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat -H "Authorization: Bearer <KEY>" -d '{"model":"redwood-chat-medium","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize..."}],"stream":false}'
[06:56] Maya Patel: I want to highlight retry best practices again - for non-idempotent operations avoid blind retries. Use idempotency keys for safe retries and exponential backoff.
[07:07] Samir Rao: Understood. Any monitoring or observability baked into the console?
[07:12] Jordan Lee: Yes - per-route latency histograms, token cost breakdown, and logs. You can export to Datadog or our tracing hooks.
[07:22] Priya Das: Do you have a playground that records inputs for audit?
[07:27] Maya Patel: Yes with opt-in retention. You can disable PII retention or route logs to your KMS for Private.
[07:36] Samir Rao: Ok, let's talk timeline: we want a POC in the next 2-3 weeks. Who should own the kickoff?
[07:43] Maya Patel: We can run a short POC - Jordan will own the technical plan, I'll handle commercials. We'll scope a 2-week pilot with sample prompts and a small synthetic load.
[07:55] Jordan Lee: I'll prepare a benchmark plan and some scripts you can run. We'll propose test matrix: latency p50/p95, cost per 1k tokens, and success rate under burst.
[08:06] Leah Kim: That sounds good. Could you include recommended retry settings in the benchmark doc?
[08:10] Jordan Lee: Yes, will include recommended backoff start 500ms, max retries 5, jitter.
[08:17] Priya Das: Any notes about concurrent streams per connection?
[08:20] Jordan Lee: Our SDKs multiplex and you can open multiple streams; limits depend on network and client. For scale we recommend pooling connections.
[08:30] Maya Patel: We'll also include a sample SSO integration doc and link to SOC2 report.
[08:36] Samir Rao: Perfect.
[08:39] Maya Patel: Quick recap of next steps: I'll send pricing and security FAQ; Jordan will send the curl/SDK samples and benchmark plan; you will share prompt set and QPS targets. We'll schedule the POC scoping call for next week.
[08:56] Samir Rao: Thanks, appreciate it.
[09:00] Maya Patel: Thanks all - we'll follow up by EOD with links.
[09:05] (call ends)

Notes on transcript: occasional words mis-transcribed (e.g., KV cache recorded as "K-V cash"). Some speaker labels generic at moments when recording glitched. The conversation contained a brief simulated network hiccup for demo of retries. The transcript aligns with duration ~42 minutes with quieter blocks while demos ran.
